articles.title: My HTML-to-Markdown converter shipped tables my spreadsheet API couldn't parse — the colspan lie
articles.excerpt: Built the HTML-to-Markdown endpoint so agent pipelines could turn messy web pages into clean Markdown. Tables looked perfect in my tests: pipe tables, aligned columns, the works. Then I pointed my XLS…
articles.body: Built the HTML-to-Markdown endpoint so agent pipelines could turn messy web pages into clean Markdown. Tables looked perfect in my tests: pipe tables, aligned columns, the works. Then I pointed my XLSX converter at the output and watched it silently produce garbage — every row after a colspan was shifted one column left, and no error anywhere. Turned out the Markdown table spec has no way to express "this cell spans two columns." My converter emitted the cell text in one cell, the next cell's text in the next, and everything downstream shifted. A human reading the rendered table sees alignment; a parser reading the pipe syntax sees a table with the wrong number of columns per row. The fix wasn't in the Markdown.

articles.title: Refactoring a Distributed Cache for Strong Reads When Eventual Consistency Fails
articles.excerpt: we hit a subtle bug in our order‑service after a recent traffic surge: occasional duplicate invoices appeared in the admin UI. the root cause? a cache layer that was designed for eventual consistency…
articles.body: we hit a subtle bug in our order‑service after a recent traffic surge: occasional duplicate invoices appeared in the admin UI. the root cause? a cache layer that was designed for eventual consistency but was being used for read‑after‑write scenarios. The Problem our stack uses a Node.js API gateway, a PostgreSQL write store, and a Redis cluster as a read‑through cache. writes go through a transaction, then an async job publishes an order.updated event to a Kafka topic. the consumer updates the Redis entry. under low load the latency between the DB commit and the cache refresh is negligible, but under load the lag grows to several seconds. the UI, which reads directly from Redis for latency reasons, sometimes shows stale data, leading to duplicate processing downstream.

articles.title: Flutter Repository Pattern: Keep API Calls Out of Widgets
articles.excerpt: Open any Flutter project that has been alive for more than six months and you will find it: a widget with an http.get buried in initState, a Firestore query inside a build method, a SharedPreferences…
articles.body: Open any Flutter project that has been alive for more than six months and you will find it: a widget with an http.get buried in initState , a Firestore query inside a build method, a SharedPreferences read next to a setState . It works. And it is exactly how codebases become untestable. The Flutter repository pattern is the fix: a single class per feature that owns all data access, so your widgets never touch a network call, a database, or a cache directly. The idea is simple. Everything above the repository — your ViewModels, your widgets — asks for data through one clean interface: "give me the products." Everything below the repository — REST APIs, Firestore, local caches — is hidden behind it. When the data source changes, only the repository changes.

articles.body: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit).

articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.excerpt: 'Luckily I’m still in love with this story, and I am in love with writing it.'
articles.body: Fall has officially arrived, and as autumn leaves blaze in vivid colors, there is no better time to plunge into the imaginative world of New York Times best-selling author Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl", the wildly addictive science fantasy book series that's taking the world by storm. Even if you haven't read them, you've probably seen folks carrying these books, emblazoned with their loud, neon-colored covers, at your neighborhood coffee house. articles.title: SpaceX's Starship just turned 10 years old. When will it go to Mars?
articles.excerpt: A decade after Elon Musk publicly unveiled plans for the fully reusable megarocket, Starship has reached orbit. How far away is Mars?
articles.body: Starship just reached orbit for the first time, carrying satellites for SpaceX's Starlink program. Analysts disagree on whether that's a detour or the destination — and what of the company's plans for the Red Planet? Ten years ago, Elon Musk stood on stage at the International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Guadalajara, Mexico, and unveiled plans for a giant spaceship to carry people to Mars. This past Sept. 28 — a decade and a day later — the descendant of that vehicle reached orbit for the first time , on Starship's 14th-ever test flight. The designs and hardware evolved greatly over those 10 years.

Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters. A paper describing the findings, led by Andrea Botteon of the National Institute for Astrophysics, or INAF, in Italy, published Wednesday in the Astronomy & Astrophysics journal .

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Chuck Yeager was a test pilot for the U.S. Air Force who made history by flying an aircraft faster than the speed of sound. Yeager made his historic flight in a Bell X-1 rocket plane that he named "Glamorous Glennis" after his wife. Yeager had broken two ribs the night before when he fell off a horse, but that didn't stop him! His aircraft was dropped from a Boeing B-29 bomber before accelerating to a speed of Mach 1.07, which is about 821 mph (1,321 km/h). The speed of sound, Mach 1, is about 760 mph (1,223 km/h). USAF Capt. Charles E. Yeager (shown standing with the Bell X-1 supersonic rocket plane) became the first man to fly faster than the speed of sound in level flight on Oct. 14, 1947.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
